questions.question: Q: How does setting function as more than just a backdrop in film?
questions.correctAnswer: Setting can operate as a character in its own right, shaping the narrative and the audience's emotional response. A cramped, cluttered interior may reflect a character's mental state, while a vast, empty landscape can convey isolation or freedom. questions.question: Q: Explain how costume can be used to show character development across a film.
questions.correctAnswer: Costume changes can trace a character's arc visually. At the start, a character may wear drab, constricting clothes reflecting repression or low status. As they gain confidence or power, costume may become bolder in colour, more fitted or more expressive. questions.question: Q: What is the significance of iconography in genre film?
questions.correctAnswer: Iconography provides a visual shorthand that audiences recognise instantly, setting expectations and creating pleasure through familiarity. In horror, iconography includes dark houses, knives, masks and shadows; in sci-fi, it includes futuristic technology, spaceships and dystopian cityscapes. questions.question: Q: How can the staging of actors within a scene reveal power dynamics?
questions.correctAnswer: Physical positioning communicates hierarchy and relationships. A character placed higher in the frame or physically above others conveys dominance; one isolated at the edge of the frame suggests marginalisation. questions.question: Q: Why is it important to consider what is absent from the mise-en-scene as well as what is present?
questions.correctAnswer: What is deliberately excluded from the frame can be as meaningful as what is included. An empty chair may signify loss or absence; a character's bare, impersonal room may reveal emotional emptiness. Excluding certain objects or colours can create unease or highlight what a character lacks. questions.correctAnswer: The mise-en-scene creates meaning through a carefully constructed combination of setting, props, costume, makeup and performance that establishes a world of social division and personal desperation. The setting is a cramped, dimly lit apartment with peeling wallpaper and minimal furniture, immediately communicating poverty and neglect. The worn fabric of the sofa and the empty fridge function as props that reinforce the character's economic hardship without dialogue. The protagonist's faded, oversized coat and scuffed shoes contrast sharply with the crisp, tailored suit of the visitor, visually encoding the power imbalance between them. Makeup enhances this contrast: the protagonist's pallid complexion and dark circles suggest exhaustion, while the visitor appears well-groomed and healthy. The staging places the visitor standing in the centre of the room looking down at the protagonist who sits hunched on the edge of the sofa, their positions literalising the hierarchy between them. A recurring motif — a child's drawing pinned to the wall — appears in the background, its bright colours the only vibrant element in the muted palette, symbolising hope and the stakes of the encounter. As the scene progresses, the protagonist gradually straightens their posture, a subtle shift in performance that signals growing resolve.
